A strong crossover raise can suggest that a company has “reached a level of maturity” and could go public soon, according to Sofinnova Investments’ Jim Healy.
Crossover fundraisings this year could top 2025 in terms of both deal count and value, with PitchBook projecting $4.22 billion across 28 raises . But so far, 2025’s biggest individual rounds still top this year’s.
2025 had three of the top six highest value crossovers in biotech history, accounting for 3% of the year’s $3.83 billion total. These included Kailera Therapeutics, whose $600 million raise a year ago this month holds the number one spot. The obesity specialist followed that up with a $625 million IPO in April 2026.
“Crossover financings are the gateway to public markets,” Jim Healy, the managing partner at Sofinnova Investments, told BioSpace in an email interview. “A large crossover round can therefore indicate that a company has reached a level of maturity and institutional interest that extends beyond traditional venture investors.”
Crossovers, typically the last fundraising round before a biotech goes public, give private companies access to an expanded investor base and additional capital, acting as a “late-stage bridge to an IPO,” said Ben Zercher, senior biotech and pharma analyst at PitchBook.
That doesn’t mean that public investors don’t sometimes throw their support behind earlier-stage companies, Healy and Zercher both noted. Indeed, some of the biggest funding efforts with crossover participation involved drugmakers with no assets to their name.
These include Eikon Therapeutics, which bagged nearly $520 million in a series B in early 2022, and computation-centric insitro, which attracted a $400 million C. Both raises happened before the companies had assembled their pipelines.
Of course, earlier participation means greater risk for these public-markets investors, Healy explained. “They may be underwriting the quality of the science, management team, platform, pipeline and potential market opportunity well before the company reaches traditional public-market milestones.”
Alongside Kailera, Eikon and insitro, BioSpace here looks at biopharma’s biggest crossover rounds of all time, as collected by PitchBook.
IPO
Steady stream of crossover rounds stock biotech’s IPO pipeline
Biotech crossover rounds could top $4.22 billion across about 28 rounds this year, PitchBook forecasts.

Kailera Therapeutics
Date: Oct. 14, 2025 Deal size: $600 million Funding stage: Series B
Just months before its record-breaking $625 million IPO in April 2026, Kailera Therapeutics closed a hefty $600 million series B that counted among its participants certain public investors.
The money was meant to advance KAI-9531, a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist, into global Phase 3 development for weight loss, the company said at the time. The asset, also known as ribupatide, was originally developed by China’s Jiangsu Hengrui. Kailera acquired exclusive rights to the asset outside the Greater China region in October 2024, concurrent with the Boston biotech’s $400 million series A .
Kailera has earmarked some $625 million to support the Phase 3 testing of ribupatide and around $150 million to develop a pill form of the drug. Enrollment into the Phase 3 KaiNETIC program, which includes three studies, is ongoing, with data expected in 2028, the company said in its Q2 report in August .
Kailera has set aside about $50 million for the daily GLP-1 pill KAI-7535, also from Hengrui. In July, topline Phase 3 data from a study conducted in China demonstrated 9.5% and 10.9% mean weight reduction at 44 weeks for the 120-mg and 180-mg doses, respectively, as compared with 2.5% in placebo. In a July 7 note, analysts at William Blair said they were “particularly alarmed” by the high rates of nausea and vomiting in patients treated with KAI-7535 versus placebo.
Kailera’s stock dipped in the days following the readout and has continued a steady downward trend that started as soon as it hit the public markets. All told, shares are down 54% since the IPO.
The company has launched a global Phase 2 trial for KAI-7535, with topline data expected next year, according to the Q2 report.

Eikon Therapeutics
Date: Jan. 6, 2022 Deal size: $517.8 million Funding stage: Series B
Eikon Therapeutics is a prime example of how a company can drum up substantial crossover support even before unveiling a pipeline. In early 2022, the California biotech brought in $517.8 million in a series B round .
At the core of Eikon’s pitch is its proprietary platform, which uses advanced imaging, high-performance computing and robotics to characterize how proteins interact inside cells. The series B proceeds went towards this platform as well as several discovery programs, though the biotech at the time didn’t identify specific disease targets or areas of priority.
In June 2023, the startup acquired a portfolio of drug candidates, including TLR7/8 immune modulators from Seven and Eight Biotherapeutics, PARP1-selective blockers from Impact Therapeutics and a host of preclinical assets from Cleave Therapeutics. Two of these—the TLR7/8 asset EIK1001 and the PARP1 candidate EIK1003—are now the biotech’s most mature molecules , with both undergoing Phase 2 studies.
Laronde
Date: Aug. 30, 2021 Deal size: $440 million Funding stage: Series B
Like Eikon, Laronde attracted early crossover interest and drew in public investors for its $440 million series B in August 2021—the biotech’s first external financing effort.
At the time, the company earmarked the money to advance its endless RNA platform, which allows prolonged and continuous expression of proteins to address various pathologies. The series B proceeds were also meant to help the Flagship Pioneering–founded company develop a pipeline of therapies across a wide variety of indications, though the biotech didn’t specify priority targets.
Investors’ early bet on Laronde didn’t pan out, however, at least not by way of an IPO. In October 2023—amid the fallout of a STAT News investigation about data integrity problems underpinning the biotech’s massive series B—Laronde merged with Flagship’s Senda Biosciences to form Sail Biomedicines. The merger’s financial details were not disclosed.
Laronde’s series B involved Flagship, as well as other investors like T. Rowe Price Associates, Invus and accounts managed by BlackRock. Sail continues to operate privately under Flagship.
Tubulis
Date: Oct. 30, 2025 Deal size: €344 million ($401 million) Funding stage: Series C
In October 2025, Tubulis’ series C round topped $400 million , thanks in part to the participation of a number of public backers.
Crossover buzz for Tubulis at the time was driven by the biotech’s next-generation antibody-drug conjugate TUB-040, designed to target a protein found on the surface of cells that helps maintain phosphate concentrations. This target, called NaPi2b , is highly expressed in a variety of tumors.
Days before closing the series C round, Tubulis presented Phase 1/2a data for TUB-040, touting a 59% overall response rate in heavily pretreated patients with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. The capital raised was earmarked for the expansion of TUB-040’s development program, including exploring earlier lines of treatment and other solid tumor indications. Aside from ovarian cancer, TUB-040 is also in Phase 1/2 testing for non-small cell lung cancer.
Tubulis gave investors a pretty happy ending when Gilead in April acquired the company for $3.15 billion upfront plus up to $1.85 billion in milestones.

Insitro
Date: March 15, 2021 Deal size: $400 million Funding stage: Series C
Insitro, the other company that generated crossover interest in the absence of a pipeline, roped in a number of public backers for its $400 million series C in March 2021.
At the time, insitro’s main appeal was driven by its machine learning platform, designed to overcome key bottlenecks in drug development, the biotech said . In particular, the biotech used its computation-heavy approach to discover potential therapeutic targets and segment patient populations for better clinical strategies.
Insitro mostly dedicated the series C proceeds to expanding this platform and opening up access to enabling datasets and complementary technologies. The company also planned to set aside some of the money for potentially in-licensed assets.
Indeed, since the series C, insitro has added wholly owned investigational therapies to its pipeline—largely enabled by an alliance with Eli Lilly. The companies in October 2024 entered into a trio of agreements : Two deals gave the biotech access to a delivery technology for liver-directed siRNA therapies, while the third focused on an unspecified metabolic disease. No financial details were disclosed.
Insitro’s pipeline also includes an ALS program in collaboration with Bristol Myers Squibb, obesity assets enabled by Lilly and a wholly in-house project for dry age-related macular degeneration.
Insitro remains a private company.
Eikon Therapeutics
Date: Feb. 26, 2025 Deal size: $350.7 million Funding stage: Series D
Eikon makes a second appearance on this list with a funding round more than three years after its 2021 series B raise that attracted crossover interest. In February 2025, the biotech corralled another $350.7 million in a series D raise, once again pulling in public investors.
Crossover buzz was more typical for this round, with Eikon being much nearer to an IPO; just under a year later, the company went public with a raise that topped $380 million .

Eikon earmarked the series D proceeds for EIK1001 and EIK1003, though the biotech at the time also pointed to EIK1004, another PARP1 inhibitor that can penetrate the central nervous system and is being tested for brain cancers.
These assets were at the heart of Eikon’s IPO as well, according to a securities filing at the time. Around $100 million went to EIK1001, pushing the asset through the Phase 2 portion of its Phase 2/3 program in melanoma, as well as supporting the molecule’s advancement in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). EIK1001’s melanoma program is underway , while a registrational Phase 2/3 study in NSCLC kicked off in July.
EIK1003 received some $60 million to carry it through Phase 1/2 development, while EIK1004 got $40 million to help complete the Phase 1 portion of a Phase 1/2 trial. These programs are ongoing .

All-New Audi A6 Allroad Estate Model Hits the Streets in this Region, and This Is How Much It Costs
49 photos
Photo: Audi
The adventurer from the premium German brand from Ingolstadt, the Audi A6 Allroad, comes to the Land Down Under starting from AU$127,900, which is the equivalent of almost $90k at the current exchange rate.
Audi in Australia has been pretty consistent with the novelties: in September they announced the refined Q6 e-tron and SQ6 e-tron models with better specifications and new pricing; in August they introduced to the range the all-electric Q4 e-tron models with improved technical specifications, and back in July they revealed the all-new Audi Q9 that is also coming to the Land Down Under .
Now, in October, the fifth generation of the Audi A6 Allroad is coming to Australia with “a striking new wide-body design with the versatility, comfort, and capability synonymous with the Allroad nameplate.” For the local market, there will be two electrified powertrains, and it’s also the most “comprehensively equipped A6 Allroad to date, with standard adaptive air suspension, all-wheel steering, panoramic glass roof with switchable transparency, and next-generation digital technology.”
Audi Australia has revealed the pricing and specification for the new iteration, which has been redesigned from the ground up alongside the regular A6 sedan and estate models, but comes as a more adventurous proposition with standard quattro all-wheel drive, adaptive air suspension, and all-wheel steering offered standard across the range.
For the Australian market, the family will have two siblings: A6 Allroad quattro e-hybrid, starting from AU$127,900, as well as the mild hybrid A6 Allroad TDI quattro , with pricing for the latter starting from AU$137,900, which is the equivalent of almost $97k at the current exchange rate.
The PHEV model combines the well-known 2.0-liter TFSI gasoline engine with an electric motor for a total combined output of 270 kW and 500 Nm. That’s 362 hp and 369 lb-ft of torque, by the way. There’s also a big 25.9 kWh battery pack, enabling an electric driving range of up to 87 km (54 miles), but it’s only combined with AC charging.
The e-hybrid is distinguished by the 21-inch Audi Sport alloy wheels and red brake calipers. The other option is the TDI quattro with a 3.0-liter turbo diesel and 220 kW plus 580 Nm (295 hp and 428 lb-ft) of torque, featuring Audi's latest mild hybrid plus technology.
The standard specification includes Matrix LED headlights and LED rear lights, while the optional Premium package adds digital Matrix LED headlights with micro-LED technology and digital OLED rear lights. Other perks include adaptive air suspension, all-wheel steering, the S Line interior, electrically adjustable front seats, a panoramic glass roof with switchable transparency, or the optional Customised contour seats package.
The technology package contains an 11.9-inch Audi virtual cockpit plus, a 14.5-inch OLED MMI touch display, as well as a standard 10.9-inch MMI front passenger display along with Audi connect plus, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, or a Bang & Olufsen 3D Premium Sound System, featuring 16 speakers, including a subwoofer, and a total output of 685 watts.
"The Audi A6 Allroad has always occupied a distinctive position in our portfolio, combining the practicality of an Avant with the confidence and capability of quattro all-wheel drive," said Peter Strudwicke, Audi Australia Product Manager for the A6 Allroad. "This new generation takes that formula further, with a more striking, purposeful design, an exceptional level of standard equipment, and a sophisticated chassis that makes the A6 Allroad equally suited to everyday driving and longer journeys across Australia."

Compensation can feel like a verdict on your value. Executive coach Angela Justice explains why companies are usually pricing the job, not the person doing it—and how understanding the difference can help you make better career decisions.
That’s less than I make now.
The recruiter had just shared the salary range for a role she was genuinely interested in. Same level. More appealing work. A company she liked. But the top of the range was $20,000 below her current base.
Her reaction was immediate. They don’t understand what I’m worth. Except that was not what the recruiter had told her. The company had communicated what the job was worth to them.
That distinction is easy to understand intellectually and much harder to hold onto when the number is yours. We spend years building expertise, judgment and experience, then naturally look to salary as evidence of what all of that adds up to. But companies are usually answering a narrower question: What do we need to pay to get this work done by someone who can do it?
Better at your job does not always mean better paid
We want compensation to behave like a scoreboard. Stronger performer, higher pay. More experience, higher pay. Greater contribution, higher pay.
It does not work that way.
A job’s price is shaped by the scope of the role, how difficult the expertise is to find, what employers are paying for it and how much the company needs that capability at that particular moment. That means two directors at the same company can be paid differently even if the lower-paid one has more experience or a stronger performance. Their jobs may draw from different talent markets. One capability may be harder to find, more expensive to replace or in greater demand across the industry.
Most of us understand this in the abstract. It is much harder when the comparison involves someone we know. Then we stop comparing jobs and start comparing people. Why does she make more than I do? Does the company think he is more important? Am I not as highly regarded as I thought?
Higher pay starts to look like a ranking.
Sometimes, it may reflect a real difference in scope or contribution. Sometimes, there is an inequity. But sometimes, the company simply has to pay more for one kind of work than another.
Are you underpaid, or is the work priced lower?
There are two problems that can feel almost identical when you are the one looking at the paycheck.
The first is being underpaid for the job you are doing. If comparable roles consistently pay more, your responsibilities have expanded without your compensation following or people doing genuinely similar work are earning more, you may have a compensation problem.
The second is the job you are doing does not pay what you want to earn. That possibility is uncomfortable because it separates excellence from economics. You can be exceptional at work the market prices lower. That does not make the work less important, and it does not make someone in a higher-paying role more capable. It means employers are willing to pay different amounts for different kinds of work.
Those two situations call for different responses that inform career decisions. The first may justify a compensation discussion, a leveling conversation or eventually a change of employer. The second sparks a broader question: Are the economics of this kind of work consistent with what I want from my career?
The answer does not have to be “No.” You may love the work. You may value the mission, the flexibility, the people or other parts of the job more than maximizing compensation. But you can make a better career decision when you know which tradeoff you are actually making.
What else are you getting from the job?
Compensation is not the only economic value of a role.
In biotech, a smaller company may give you access to experiences you might wait years to get elsewhere: an initial public offering, an acquisition, a financing, taking an asset into development or building a function from scratch. Those experiences can change what you bring to the next employer.
Large pharma can build a different kind of value. You may learn how strong systems and processes work, how decisions get made across a complex organization, how to operate with rigor at scale or what a mature function looks like. That experience can be especially useful later in a company that needs to build those things.
Different environments build different capabilities . A useful way to evaluate a role is what you will walk away with when it ends.
So, if your compensation disappoints you, ask what else you are accumulating. Is the role giving you experience, exposure or responsibility that may expand your options later? While that does not erase a pay problem, it does make the calculation more complete.
Ask what the number is actually telling you
“Know your worth” sounds empowering. As compensation advice, it is not especially useful. It assumes there is some number attached to your professional value waiting for the right employer to discover it.
There isn’t.
The same person can command very different compensation depending on the work, the market, the company and the problem they are being hired to solve.
So, when a salary number bothers you, do not immediately turn it into a judgment about yourself. First, separate the number from the meaning you are assigning to it. Are you underpaid for the work? Is the work itself priced lower than you want to be paid? Or are you in a role that is building experience likely to change your options later?
Your company is not paying you what you are worth. It is paying for the work it needs from you. Once you understand the difference, you can decide what, if anything, you want to do about it.

Google Announces New Android Auto Feature That Could Make Users Love or Hate Gemini
6 photos
Photo: Google
Google has just confirmed that Gemini is now available globally on Android Auto and Android Automotive, so Google Assistant is part of the history now. That’s why the search giant believes this is the right moment to introduce a new feature.
Personal Intelligence is coming to Android Auto and cars with Google built-in, and at first glance, it’s the kind of feature that could make users love the new assistant or hate it even more. That’s because Gemini has so far been a letdown for many Android Auto users , mainly due to glitches that prevented it from running even the most basic tasks.
The purpose of Personal Intelligence is simple: it’s trying to make Gemini an even more personal assistant, and to do this, it gets access to the rest of the Google applications that you already installed and use on your phone.
These include Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Maps, YouTube, and even Google Photos.
Why it needs access to all these apps? Because that’s the only way Gemini can become truly personal, as it needs more information about your emails, the videos you watch, the locations you visited, and your past and upcoming appointments.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Using information collected from these apps, Gemini can offer more relevant answers when being prompted to look for something in your car.
For example, if you’re on the road and want to make sure you won’t miss your flight, you can ask Google about the departure time and possible delays.
You don’t have to provide any specifics, as it’s enough to ask about your flight, with Gemini searching other Google services, such as Gmail, for flight information. It can look for an email where your flight was confirmed, extract the departure time, look it up online, search for any delays, and then offer a detailed answer right on your Android Auto screen.
The best thing about this feature is that you can speak naturally, so you don’t need to remember any phrases. Once Gemini can access the rest of the Google apps, it can figure out what you mean, and if it needs more information, it’ll ask for it.
Gemini isn’t limited to just one service at a time, so if your request includes information from multiple apps, it’ll look everywhere for a complete answer.
For example, you can tell Gemini to find the coffee place in the photo submitted by a friend (and saved in Google Photos) and set navigation to its address. The assistant will load the gallery, look for recent photos with a coffee place, figure out more details to determine its location, and then launch Google Maps to configure navigation to the address it found online.
Another big feature is the ability to keep your conversations and continue from where you left off. As you drive with Android Auto on the screen, you can ask Gemini about a request you submitted in previous days, and the assistant will remember it.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Without a doubt, many people might be concerned that Personal Intelligence is a way to surrender all their privacy and let artificial intelligence be in control of their lives.
Google says these concerns shouldn’t exist because users are always in control of what they share and how they share.
“Your apps aren’t connected until you choose to turn it on, and you can turn it off anytime in your Gemini settings. And cars with Google built-in only share personal responses when you’re in the car with your phone connected,” Google says.
But probably the most important part is that Personal Intelligence is not tied to a specific feature integrated into Gemini. This means that if you want to use Gemini without activating this new feature, you can very well do so without facing any restrictions. Sure, it wouldn’t be such a big surprise to see this changing in the long term, but for now, you can enjoy the rest of the Gemini feature arsenal without having to enable Personal Intelligence.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The only difference is that “answers won’t be tailored to you,” as Google itself puts it. You’ll lose the personal part of artificial intelligence.
The rollout of these new capabilities has already started on Android Auto, while users running the new AI-powered assistant in a car with Google built-in will have to wait a little bit longer. Google says Personal Intelligence will land in these cars in the coming months, so expect it to show up in early 2027.
There’s one important mention, though. Personal Intelligence is only available for users who are at least 18 years old and can be used exclusively with personal Google accounts. This means that if you use Workspace business, enterprise, or education accounts, Personal Intelligence won’t be available on your device.
Google doesn’t tie the release of this feature to a specific Android Auto version, but you should still keep the app up to date to receive the latest fixes and improvements.

Tesla and SpaceX have both formed special committees within their corporate boards to explore the possibility of merging the two companies according to Elon Musk, who is CEO of both companies.
The merger could have big consequences not just for Tesla and SpaceX shareholders, but could dilute the retirement savings of everyone with exposure to major stock indices.
SpaceX held its quarterly earnings call today, just a few months after going public for the first time.
And for us in the electric car world, the big and unsurprising news was that Tesla and SpaceX are now formally reviewing the possibility of merging the companies together.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The possibility of a merger has been rumored for a long time. Musk has long complained of the need to respond to shareholders’ concerns as CEO of Tesla. It is odd, then, for him to take SpaceX public when he has complained for more than a decade about Tesla being public and having to respond to shareholders.
Musk wants more control
The problem, as Musk sees it, is that he does not have enough control of Tesla. Over the years, his ownership percentage had dwindled as Tesla sold stock in offerings or granted stock to employees, though today after the restoration of his illegal pay package , his ownership percentage runs around 22%.
This means he can’t ram anything through that he wants, he has to build consensus around his ideas. (That said, shareholders have proven themselves happy to oblige any ridiculous idea that he proposes to them…)
But that’s not enough for Musk. He wants total control of the company, and he’ll try any financial shenanigans to get it. He’s gone so far as to market this idea by saying that he needs $1 trillion so he can control a robot army .
If he gets that most recent pay package, a huge chunk of shares will be created out of thin air, going right into the pocket of the one person on the planet who needs them the least , and diluting the voting power and value of every other person’s shares.
A marketing plan gets him there
So, he cooked up a plan. Sell the most ridiculous CEO pay package ever devised to Tesla shareholders, making big claims that the stock will only be delivered if Tesla manages to deliver a million robots, a million robotaxis, and various other operational milestones that would surely indicate Tesla’s success as a company.
Then do the same with SpaceX, promising to put a million colonists on Mars (which will not happen ). Make sure to give yourself super-voting shares before SpaceX goes public, so you don’t have to worry about ever listening to anyone else.
Let these high-profile targets grab headlines, and trick shareholders who don’t know any better into voting for these pay packages , thinking they’re safe because even if their shares are diluted by these massive stock grants, they’ll just end up with a slightly smaller piece of a much larger pie. It’s a win-win, right?
Shareholders were tricked with impossible promises
Well… unless we include a provision in the pay package that says the shares are automatically delivered in the case of a merger . That’s right, if SpaceX and Tesla merge, then all the talk about robots and Mars colonies is irrelevant. Musk gets his stock regardless of any operational milestones.
He gets stock, you get diluted, and you didn’t even see a single robot delivered.
And so, after only the second quarterly report ever presented by SpaceX, the companies are already exploring the possibility of merging.
Musk said today during SpaceX’s earnings call that each company has formed a “special committee” of “independent board members” (and those quotes around the word “independent” are doing heavy lifting) which are reviewing the possibility of a merger.
“Independent” boards oddly always side with Musk over shareholders
This does not mean that the merger is a certain thing. First, the “independent” board members need to agree that it’s a good idea – but, given that Tesla’s board has always sought Musk’s interests and not those of the company , it certainly seems that if Musk thinks it’s a good idea, the committee probably will too.
After all, the special committee on pay signed off on Musk’s ridiculous trillion-dollar pay package , despite that all that package did was attach the company to the very anchor that is dragging it down . That package would benefit Musk at the cost of all other shareholders and the company’s own operations, so the board’s independence is called into question if that’s the kind of idea it signs off on.
Musk is not officially allowed to be involved in these discussions, nor are boardmembers not deemed “independent,” like his brother, Kimbal Musk. But Elon has made it clear that he wants this to happen. He did so again today, when he said that he thinks a merger would be a good idea, because “we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity” (notably, we are not, and neither would that be particularly relevant to an auto manufacturer).
So, a board sign-off seems reasonably certain given what Musk has publicly directed Tesla’s captured board to do. After that, shareholders of both companies need to approve the move.
Will the shareholder vote pass? Tesla laid the groundwork
For SpaceX this is an easy one – Musk controls more than 50% of voting shares, and therefore the company will approve of the merger. He set it up this way, and the merger would give him more money and more control, so he’s going to vote for it.
For Tesla, the vote could theoretically fail to pass. The company would need a vote of 50% of all outstanding shares, not just 50% of shareholders who turn out to cast their votes.
For this reason, Tesla has already prepared a questionable “auto-vote” procedure . This would allow shareholders to set an instruction to automatically vote all of their shares with board recommendations, no matter how bad those board recommendations are to the shareholders’ own interests.
This is a big deal for Tesla, because Tesla has a larger percentage of its shares owned by retail shareholders than most companies, and retail shareholders tend to turn out in low percentages. So this is a way to encourage more retail votes – and of course, the only option is to auto-vote with the board, not to auto-vote against it.
So the stage has been set, and today, the companies took the first formal step towards making this merger happen.
Not the first time Musk has tricked shareholders into a bad merger
This wouldn’t be the first merger that Musk has tricked shareholders into.
Back in 2016, Musk went on stage to demonstrate slick-looking Tesla solar roof tiles, which would be more durable than a regular roof and generate energy along the way, meaning they’d have a lower total cost of ownership.
Those solar roof tiles never made it onto the market in any significant numbers, and Tesla eventually killed the product in August of this year .
But they served their purpose – they served to sell Tesla shareholders on the idea of purchasing SolarCity, a solar startup founded by Elon Musk’s cousins, Lyndon and Peter Rive. It also allowed billions of debt from SolarCity to be absorbed by Tesla. (Hey, that kind of sounds like when Musk bought twitter for $30 billion more than it was worth, funded it with debt, shuffled that debt into SpaceX, then IPOed to offload the debt onto the public)
And now, both Tesla and SpaceX are selling their shareholders on the idea of a merger, just a week after Musk hosted a ridiculous product demo of a product that has been delayed 11 years after it was first announced, and is now being shown off in a form that will never be legal to drive on public roads. Sounds a little familiar, doesn’t it?
This would dilute Tesla/SpaceX shareholders, but also everyone’s retirement plan
All of this seems like it would only be of interest to Tesla and SpaceX shareholders, but the fact of the matter is, that means it’s of interest to all of us.
The companies are two of the largest in America by market cap, which means they are included in major stock indices. And many retirement funds thus hold exposure to Tesla, and have for years.
SpaceX is a different story, since it’s a brand-new stock. Given that it just IPOed a few months ago, it wouldn’t normally be added to indices for another year. But Musk got the rules changed so that SpaceX would be included in the Nasdaq 100 index just days after IPO, which in turn means it might already be in your retirement portfolio .
So both companies are in a lot of retirement plans, and the value of those shares will be diluted by giving a bigger share of each company to Musk if the two companies merge.
And thus, everyone with a retirement account would be forced to contribute money to this non-performing “performance” award for a guy whose main interest, if you read his output on the platform he treats as a full-time job , is to use his unearned wealth to impose white supremacy and do things that are, and I quote one Elon Musk on this one: “ not good for America or the world .”
Oh, he’s also suing to defend nude deepfakes made without consent . Hope you like your retirement money being used for that.
We wrote last October that “ Elon Musk’s $1 trillion pay day gets more ridiculous the more you look into it ,” and, well, it looks like the vote wasn’t the end of it.

When Segway launched the original Xyber last year , it was one of those e-bikes that immediately turned heads. With its futuristic styling, oversized frame, and high-performance off-road ambitions, it looked more like a concept vehicle than something you could actually buy.
Now the company is hoping to capture a much wider audience with the new Segway Xyber Air, a lighter, street-legal version that keeps much of the original’s aggressive styling while fitting neatly into the familiar Class 1, 2, and 3 e-bike categories.
At first glance, you’d be forgiven for mistaking the Xyber Air for its larger sibling. It retains the angular frame design and moto-inspired proportions that made the original stand out, complete with Segway’s signature X-shaped front and rear lighting.
But beneath the familiar styling is a much more approachable machine.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Power comes from a 750W nominal rear hub motor producing 80 Nm of torque, with peak output reaching 1,600W.
Riders can choose between Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 operation depending on local regulations, with speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in Class 1 and 2 modes or 28 mph (45 km/h) in Class 3.
Segway has even included a Hybrid Mode that allows throttle operation up to 20 mph while pedal assist continues to 28 mph without requiring riders to switch between ride modes.
That’s still kosher in many states, but some are starting to require true Class 3 e-bikes to have no throttle operation at all, so check your local regulations to make sure you’re compliant.
The bike is powered by a 717 Wh battery that Segway claims can deliver up to 58 miles (93 km) of range, though as always, real-world mileage will depend heavily on rider weight, terrain, and how enthusiastically that throttle gets used.
Suspension duties are handled by an 80 mm dual-crown front fork, paired with 20×4-inch fat tires and hydraulic disc brakes with 180 mm rotors.
The bike also borrows several features more commonly associated with motorcycles, including traction control, hill-start assist, regenerative hill descent control, and automatic lighting.
Whether or not an e-bike requires traction control or hill hold remains to be seen, but it’s neat to know that such moto-inspired tech is heading into the e-bike space.
Segway continues to lean heavily into connected features as well. The Xyber Air includes AirLock automatic unlocking, Apple Find My compatibility, GPS tracking, Lost Mode remote disabling, over-the-air updates, and a full-color TFT display with navigation and smartphone integration.
Some connected services will require a subscription after the first year, which is unfortunately becoming a trend in the micromobility world, but makes sense given the data connection required for those services. Still, it’d be nice to see more of a grace period, like two to three years, for connected features, since it’s not like we’re downloading gigabyte-heavy movies on our bikes.
Despite all of those features, components, and tech, the Xyber Air weighs a claimed 84 lb (38 kg), which is noticeably lighter than the original Xyber, while still supporting a 330 lb (150 kg) payload. It’s also UL 2271 and UL 2849 certified.
Sure, 84 pounds is a lot of poundage for an e-bike, but compared to the moto-styled original, it’s on a significant diet.
Ordering is now open now at a launch price of $1,999 .
Bikes are expected to begin shipping on October 27 through Segway’s dealer network and SCHEELS locations nationwide.
Electrek’s Take
I actually think Segway made the right move here.
The original Xyber had that cool flair to it, but it also blurred the line between e-bike and electric motorcycle, or shot right past it in many places. The Xyber Air looks like Segway took a step back and asked, “What if we kept the styling that people liked but made it fit within the existing e-bike framework?”
Basically, they kept the “Let’s take a shot at SUPER73” mindset but aimed for a more acceptable format considering today’s regulatory landscape.
The result is still unmistakably moto-inspired, but it’s also something that can legally access bike infrastructure in many places instead of existing in a regulatory gray area. At under $2,000, it also lands at a price point that opens the door to a larger audience.
It’s still not going to compete against the value proposition in something like the Juiced Scrambler , either in hardtail or full-suspension format, but it definitely looks like a fun ride. And with more options for more riders, there’s always going to be something for everyone!

China may be taking the majority of licensing deals this year but those transactions don’t tell the whole story, according to Locust Walk, which points to the spike in M&A among U.S. biotechs as leveling the playing field.
The rise of licensing deals with Chinese biotechs has left U.S.-based companies and leaders wringing their hands, but the onslaught of deals has come as American companies have experienced a renaissance of M&A—an exit option not open to the Chinese startups.
China’s share of global licensing deal value has risen to 58% in 2026, according to a new report from global investment bank Locust Walk. The U.S., meanwhile, has fallen from 56% in 2024 to 26% this year.
But at the same time, M&A has taken off in the U.S. biotech sector. Total deal value has already hit $173 billion through the end of the third quarter, compared to $151 billion for all of 2025. Of the 2026 total, 91% of all M&A deal value was for U.S.-headquartered companies, compared to just 1% for Chinese firms. In terms of deal volume, 78% of companies were American across the 89 total deals so far, compared to 6% for China.
As American leaders search for ways to respond to China’s ascendent homegrown industry, these differences are key to reframing the debate about whether the U.S. is actually losing ground, Locust Walk CEO Geoff Meyerson told BioSpace in an interview.
CHINA
Webinar: The China question: Can US biotechs lead as investment heads east?
In this webinar, BioSpace will gathered experts to discuss China’s impact on the future of biotech and how both U.S. and Chinese companies can thrive—and maybe even collaborate.
October 15, 2026
·
1 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
Chinese biotechs “view licensing as a fundraising event, as comparable to doing an IPO, as comparable to doing a venture round,” Meyerson said. “The U.S. is very different. You would never sell a clinical stage asset that was still your main focus. You might sell an earlier asset to fund your lead asset, but you’re never going to do that for your lead.”
U.S. biotechs can raise a venture capital round, go public or sell. These funding opportunities are less open to Chinese biotechs that have mostly pivoted to seeking out milestone-heavy licensing deals as interest in the region has soared. Venture capital in particular has plummeted for China biotechs from the highs of 2020 and 2021, Meyerson noted. M&A exits are similarly harder to come by in the Asian country.
Nevertheless, the Chinese government took steps last week to tighten rules around biotech ownership transfers, particularly for technologies related to cell and gene therapy, small nucleic acid drugs and pathogenic microorganisms. With so few M&A deals happening with foreign buyers and an exception for licensing deals, the policy change isn’t expected to have much impact.
“There’s structural reasons why M&A in China is harder because of the government and because of all different constituencies,” Meyerson explained. “But fundamentally, if you want to do a deal with a U.S. company for their lead asset, you’re buying the company.”
So the trajectory of China-based licensing deals is dramatic—but only tells half of the story. When the M&A picture is brought into focus, Meyerson said the year has actually been pretty good for U.S. companies, too.
“M&A has been on a tear this year,” Meyerson said, pointing to that $173 billion total.
The spike is not surprising, Meyerson added. When President Donald Trump began his term, the macroeconomic factors began to change in favor of buyouts after tighter regulation under President Joe Biden. While Trump has continued his predecessor’s mission to lower drug prices, regulatory pressures overall have eased.
China
China’s surging biotech sector represents both competition and lifeline for the US
As Chinese companies push beyond “me-too” drugs and the country lays out a new five-year plan targeting a $522 billion–strong biotech industry by 2030, experts say more predictable funding and regulation could help the U.S. maintain its edge.
September 23, 2026
·
8 min read
·
Shawna Williams
Read more
Meyerson also noted that China and U.S. companies have major differences in how they assess licensing deal value. Chinese companies don’t mind accepting larger downstream milestones, as evidenced by Roche’s Monday deal with Hansoh Pharmaceutical worth $400 million upfront but a potential $15 billion on the backend. U.S. biotechs, on the other hand, want a bigger upfront.
Through Q3, Locust Walk found that China’s average total 2026 deal licensing value was $2.2 billion as compared to $1 billion for U.S. companies. But U.S. sellers had a larger portion of upfront payments, representing 10% of total deal value as opposed to China’s 6%.
“In the vast majority of deals, you never receive all the milestones,” Meyerson said. “That number gets the attention. My judgment is the upfront number is actually what matters because that’s what you can feed your development programs, not smoke and mirrors.”
Royalties also don’t tend to be a major factor in Chinese licensing deals, Meyerson added. “They don’t care as much about royalties as compared to the U.S. because it’s so far downstream. They’re trying to live to fight another day to have money to fund their next development programs.”

2026 Paris Motor Show • OMODA 4 Lands in Paris To Showcase Futuristic Styling, Looks Like a Discount Urus
Chery Group International User Summit Features the World Premiere of the All-New Omoda X Adventurer
12 photos
Photo: Omoda Jaecoo Australia
The Chery Group International User Summit allowed the sibling brands Omoda Jaecoo to also take center stage during the event, and Omoda launched X, its newest adventure SUV.
Subdivisions of Chery International, part of the Chery Automobile group, a Chinese vehicle manufacturer, Omoda and Jaecoo have been established since 2022 as sibling brands that only sell vehicles outside of China. Omoda and Jaecoo entered various international regions a little later: Australia in 2023, Europe in 2024, and South Africa or Mexico also in 2023.
Now, Omoda Jaecoo are a constant presence in Australia , where they have deals with entities like Uber for their drivers to use the eligible vehicles, constantly receive various awards like the Jaecoo J5 EV being recognized in the 2026 Australian Good Design Awards, partner with the Red Bull Wings Cup, or bring together owners with the My OJ Club.
They also don’t neglect new model introductions, and back in September the company announced two all-new Omoda SUVs for Australia: Omoda 4 and Omoda 7, which are coming in 2027 below the Omoda 9 flagship after they were unveiled locally at Everything Electric Sydney. Now, at the recent Chery Group International User Summit, Omoda Jaecoo also hosted Omoda X Night, which was an event dedicated to the global reveal of Omoda’s latest model dubbed “X”.
The new model is a true ‘crossover’: it strives to combine the “everyday practicality of an SUV, the adventurous spirit of an off-road vehicle and the dynamic character of a sports car.” Omoda wants to expand the possibilities of its CUV range and bring a new automotive choice for adventure-focused customers.
The model’s design seeks inspiration from the futuristic ‘mecha culture’, according to the company, and the Omoda X “brings power, technology and a vision of the future into its design.” The designers cooked up a wide-body stance featuring “broad shoulders, a tightly sculpted waistline and a sporty silhouette,” all to create “a sense of power.”
The new model is also positioned below the Omoda 9 and measures 4,650 mm (183 inches) in length, 1,910 mm (75.19 inches) in width, and has a height of 1,720 mm or 67.71 inches. To support its adventure-focused design, the new CUV has 19-inch alloy wheels with rugged all-terrain tires, 200 mm or 7.87 inches of ground clearance, and can go through areas of water thanks to its wading depth of over 700 mm (27.55 inches). Also, towing capacity is 1,800 kg or 3,968 pounds, while inside there are no less than 39 storage spaces “providing more room for equipment for outdoor activities.”
The cabin has the so-called ‘Mecha Command Cockpit’, featuring a twin-wing layout and X-shaped floating center console. There is a 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster and a 13.2-inch central touchscreen, but the Chinese have also listened to customers, and physical controls are available for AC and driving modes, for example. Both 2WD and AWD options will be offered, alongside EV and PHEV powertrains.

Nearly $1 million in Pokémon, sports and other trading cards disappeared from a FedEx truck in Santa Ana, California. The driver discovered the missing cargo October 13 outside a Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) facility. Two pallets had vanished, and someone had removed additional packages from a third. Police are still trying to determine when and where the theft occurred.
Driver discovers missing lock at PSA facility
The FedEx vehicle was parked in a lot belonging to PSA when the driver noticed something wrong. Although the company owns the property, members of the public can access the parking area. A lock securing the rear cargo door was missing. When the driver opened the compartment, he found the contents disturbed and several shipments gone.
The driver had left the vehicle before discovering the missing lock, according to Santa Ana police. Other news outlets reported he was gone for 60 to 90 minutes. However, a department spokesperson told FreightWaves on Tuesday that investigators could not confirm that timeline. Detectives are reviewing his account to better understand the circumstances surrounding the discovery.
The driver contacted Santa Ana police, who responded to investigate the reported theft. Officers documented two missing pallets, each containing approximately 100 packages of collectible trading cards. Someone had also removed an undetermined number of parcels from a third pallet. Investigators do not yet know how many individual cards disappeared.
Police initially valued the missing merchandise at approximately $963,000, although the final loss could exceed that amount. The shipment involved collectible cards associated with PSA, which authenticates and professionally grades trading cards. Authorities have not completed a final inventory of the stolen property. That process could change the estimated value as investigators establish exactly what disappeared.
FedEx responded to FreightWaves’ request for comment with the following statement. “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation.” The company did not clarify whether FedEx was delivering cards for grading or collecting completed orders for return shipment. FreightWaves also contacted PSA to clarify the shipment’s direction and identify affected customers. The company did not respond before publication.
Southern California remained a major cargo theft hot spot during the second quarter of 2026. CargoNet reported $304.6 million in cargo theft losses during that same period. Both reports provide broader context for the financial impact of stolen freight. Neither establishes how the FedEx shipment disappeared.
Detectives return to PSA to investigate
On Tuesday, October 20, detectives returned to the PSA facility to examine potential surveillance footage and gather additional evidence. Investigators are working to corroborate the driver’s account and reconstruct the vehicle’s movements. Finding the missing cargo at PSA does not necessarily mean someone stole it there. Police have not established whether thieves accessed the vehicle in that parking lot or somewhere along its route.
Several important questions remain unanswered. Investigators have not identified suspects or determined whether thieves specifically targeted the collectible cards. Police also could not confirm whether the FedEx vehicle was a tractor-trailer, box truck or smaller delivery vehicle. The department has not announced any arrests or recovered any of the missing merchandise.
Customers concerned about missing cards should contact PSA directly, according to Santa Ana police. Authorities have not released a complete inventory identifying affected shipments. The number of customers impacted remains unknown. FreightWaves will update this story as additional details become available.
Why It Matters
Nearly $1 million in trading cards disappeared from a FedEx truck. Investigators still don’t know when or where the theft occurred. The case highlights the importance of securing unattended vehicles and maintaining a clear record of cargo movements.
